newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Philips confident on DVD encryption pact.
newsitem.headline: Philips confident on DVD encryption pact.

text.p: Philips Electronics NV said on Monday it was confident that issues hindering the widespread introduction of a new high capacity video disc technology were close to being resolved.
"It's a problem of getting people from different industries to agree," said Philips Key Modules managing director Jan Oosterveld in a telephone interview. "We're not too far off."

Oosterveld earlier delivered a speech to the Digital Video Disc (DVD) forum in Brussels saying a 10 member consortium had put forward a proposal on encryption aimed at soothing mainly movie industry qualms about pirating of its catalogues.
The consortium, which combines companies from Japan, Europe and the U.S., has come together to support a single standard. But worries remain about copyright protection.

"Various proposals are being looked at. The DVD Consortium has put a proposal on the table as well, which is based on encrypting the content," Oosterveld said. "We are confident that a solution will be agreed upon soon," he added.

"You're dealing with four or five different industry groupings. It's not only a matter of technical solutions, it's a matter of getting people with very different views working together," Oosterveld told Reuters.

Top electronics firms last year agreed on a technical format for DVD, clearing the way for a multi-billion dollar market and laying the spectre of a damaging standards battle such as the fight between rival video cassette standards in the 1980s.
DVD technology can greatly increase the amount of storage on optical discs -- one can hold the information of 12 CD-ROMS -- allowing storage of high quality image and audio on one disc.

"The interests at stake are quite clear: the software industry wants to protect their assets and we all agree that software availability will be a key to the success of DVD-Video," Oosterveld said in his speech.

Industry observers said the key issue for the global success of the format was availability of publishable material. "There's no point putting out these machines if there are no discs to put on them," said one source who declined to be named.

"Most major studios have said they will release titles once a copy protection system is agreed upon and in place," Oosterveld told industry delegates in Brussels. A copy of his speech was made available in Amsterdam.
Philips, which aims to bring out its DVD players next year, sees industry-wide sales of 250 million optical drives by 2000, 10 percent of which will be DVDs.
